module_title: Setting Aside Awards, Public Policy, and the Mediation Act 2023
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the absolute limits of judicial interference in arbitration. It breaks down the highly restrictive grounds of Section 34, the time-bound mandates of Section 29A, and the recent revolutionary Mediation Act, 2023.

core_concepts.title: Setting Aside the Arbitral Award (Section 34)
core_concepts.description:
An arbitral award is NOT open to a regular appeal. A court cannot review the merits of the case or reassess evidence. An award can only be set aside on exhaustive, strict procedural grounds:
1. Incapacity of a party.
2. Invalidity of the arbitration agreement.
3. Lack of proper notice of the appointment of the arbitrator.
4. Award deals with a dispute beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration.
5. The composition of the tribunal was not in accordance with the agreement.
6. The subject matter is not capable of settlement by arbitration under Indian law (e.g., criminal cases, divorce).
7. The award is in conflict with the **Public Policy of India**.

core_concepts.title: The 'Public Policy' & 'Patent Illegality' Thresholds
core_concepts.description:
Heavily litigated concepts defined by the Supreme Court (*Renusagar, ONGC v. Saw Pipes, Ssangyong*).
- Public Policy of India: An award violates public policy ONLY if it is induced by fraud/corruption, violates the fundamental policy of Indian law, or conflicts with the most basic notions of morality or justice.
- Patent Illegality (Section 34(2A)): Added by the 2015 amendment. A domestic award may be set aside if it is vitiated by 'patent illegality appearing on the face of the award'. However, merely an erroneous application of law or reappreciation of evidence does not constitute patent illegality.

core_concepts.title: Strict Time Limits: Section 29A
core_concepts.description:
To cure the notorious delays of Indian arbitration, the 2015 amendment inserted Section 29A.
- The Rule: The arbitral tribunal MUST make its award within **12 months** from the date the pleadings are completed.
- Extension: The parties may, by consent, extend the period for not more than **6 months**. If the award is still not made within 18 months, the mandate of the arbitrator terminates automatically, unless the Court grants a further extension (often imposing financial penalties on the slow arbitrator).

core_concepts.title: Contemporary Milestone: The Mediation Act, 2023
core_concepts.description:
A paradigm shift separating mediation from the confines of Section 89 CPC into an independent statutory regime.
- Mandate: Promotes institutional mediation. It creates the **Mediation Council of India** to regulate mediators.
- Mediated Settlement Agreement: A successfully mediated settlement signed by the parties is now legally enforceable exactly like a final court judgment or an arbitral award. Parties cannot simply walk away from a signed mediation agreement.

important_entities.name: Non-Arbitrable Disputes
important_entities.key_fact: Certain matters cannot be privately judged.
important_entities.significance: Established in *Booz Allen and Hamilton v. SBI Home Finance*. Rights *in rem* (rights against the world) are non-arbitrable, while rights *in personam* are arbitrable. Examples of non-arbitrable disputes: Criminal offenses, matrimonial disputes (divorce), insolvency and winding up of companies, and testamentary matters (validity of a will).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will claim: 'Under Section 34, the High Court can correct the mathematical or factual errors made by the Arbitrator to ensure justice.' **FALSE**. Section 34 is an application to *set aside*, NOT an appeal. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a court cannot modify or rewrite the award under Section 34. It can only quash it or uphold it.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: 12 months default + 6 months party extension. Anything beyond 18 months requires a strict Court order.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing judicial pendency, heavily cite **Section 29A of the Arbitration Act** and the **Mediation Act, 2023** as the ultimate legislative mechanisms forcing India toward a fast-track, pro-enforcement alternative dispute resolution culture.
